---
title: "Session 3: Collaboration"
---

## Overview

This session covers how to work with others on the same codebase — identifying problems, proposing fixes, and reviewing changes before they go live.

---

## Code smells

Research code is written to answer a question — not to be a software product. That's fine, but it often leaves behind patterns that make code hard to understand, re-run, or build upon.

Common code smells include:

- **Lack of comments** — it's not clear what the code is doing or why
- **Inconsistent style** — mixed naming conventions, indentation, or formatting
- **Hardcoded values** — numbers or strings that should be variables or parameters
- **Duplicate code** — the same logic repeated in multiple places instead of a function
- **Large functions** — functions that do too much and are hard to understand

::: {.callout-tip}
The process of identifying and fixing these issues is called **refactoring** — an important step before sharing your code more broadly.
:::

---

## Code review

When reviewing code — for yourself or a collaborator — look for:

🐛 **Correctness** — does it actually do what it claims? Are there silent errors?

🏷️ **Clarity** — could you understand this in six months without the author? Are comments being used in place of proper flow logic?

📊 **Visualisation** — are axes labelled? Is the palette accessible? Is the default view representative?

🔁 **Reproducibility** — are there hardcoded paths, arbitrary defaults, or missing dependencies?

✂️ **Scope** — is there dead code, repeated logic, or TODO stubs that were never addressed?

::: {.callout-tip}
You are reviewing the *code*, not the *person* (even when that person is past you!) — specific, constructive comments are always best.
:::

---

## Issues

**Issues** are GitHub's built-in way to track bugs, questions, and feature requests.

Every issue has:

- A **title** — short and specific
- A **description** — what is wrong, where, and what the expected behaviour is
- An optional **label** — e.g. `bug`, `enhancement`, `good first issue`
- An optional **assignee** — who is responsible for fixing it

::: {.callout-note}
Issues are not just bug reports — comments, decisions, and links to the fix all live in one place. As with commit messages, be specific!
:::

::: {.callout-caution}
### Exercises

3.1 Accept your GitHub collaboration invitation

3.2 Using the issue list provided, create at least one GitHub issue

3.3 Clone the repository and open it — what other smells can you find?

3.4 Record at least one more code smell as an issue
:::

---

## Branches

So far, all work has been going directly onto `main` — the live version of the code. That works fine when you are working alone. With collaborators, it creates problems:

- ❌ Two people editing the same file at the same time creates conflicts
- ❌ Half-finished changes can break the code for everyone
- ❌ No way to review work before it goes live

::: {.callout-note}
A **branch** is a safe copy of the code where you can make changes without affecting `main` — until you are ready.
:::

The typical flow:

```
main ──────────────────────────────── (always clean)
         \                    /
          fix/issue-14 ──────   (your branch)
```

::: {.callout-important}
`main` stays clean and deployable at all times by keeping work on branches.
:::

---

## Pull requests

When your branch is ready, you open a **pull request** (PR) — a request to merge your changes into `main`.

A PR lets your teammates:

- See exactly what changed, line by line
- Leave comments on specific lines
- Approve the changes — or ask for revisions
- Merge once everyone is happy

::: {.callout-tip}
One issue → one branch → one PR. Small, focused changes are much easier to review than one enormous commit.
:::

### Branch & PR workflow

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python (VSCode)

1. Click the branch name in the bottom-left status bar
2. Select **Create new branch** — name it `fix/issue-number-short-description`
3. Make your changes and commit as normal
4. Click **Publish Branch** in the Source Control tab
5. VSCode will prompt you to **Create Pull Request** — click it
6. Add a title, link to the issue (type `#` to search), and click **Create**

### R (RStudio)

1. In the **Git tab**, click the branch icon 🔀
2. Click **New Branch** — name it `fix/issue-number-short-description`
3. Make your changes and commit as normal
4. Click **Push** (↑) to push your branch to GitHub
5. GitHub will show a banner: **"Compare & pull request"** — click it
6. Add a title, link to the issue (type `#` to search), and click **Create pull request**

:::

### Reviewing & merging

1. Open the repository on GitHub
2. Click the **Pull requests** tab
3. Open the PR you have been assigned to review
4. Click **Files changed** to see the diff
5. Click `+` next to any line to leave a comment
6. When done, click **Review changes** and choose:
   - ✅ **Approve** — looks good, ready to merge
   - 💬 **Comment** — feedback but no verdict yet
   - ❌ **Request changes** — needs fixes before merging
7. Once approved → click **Merge pull request**

::: {.callout-caution}
### Exercises

3.5 Assign yourself to an open issue

3.6 Create a branch, make your changes, commit then push

3.7 Open a pull request — link it to the issue and assign a teammate as reviewer

3.8 Review a teammate's PR — leave at least one comment, then approve

3.9 Merge the approved PR and watch the live update!
:::

## Adding collaborators

A repository on GitHub is private by default — only you can see and edit it. To work with others:

1. Open your repository on GitHub
2. Go to **Settings → Collaborators**
3. Click **Add people**
4. Search by GitHub username or email
5. Set their role — **Write** is appropriate for most collaborators
6. They receive an email invitation to accept

::: {.callout-important}
Anyone with write access can push directly to `main` — which is why branches and pull requests matter.
:::

---

## Quick reference

| Action | Where |
|---|---|
| Add a collaborator | Settings → Collaborators → Add people |
| Create an issue | Issues tab → New issue → add label + assignee |
| Create a branch (VSCode) | Click branch name in status bar → New branch |
| Create a branch (RStudio) | Git tab → branch icon 🔀 → New Branch |
| Open a pull request | Push branch → GitHub banner → Compare & pull request |
| Link PR to an issue | Type `#issue-number` in the PR description |
| Review a PR | Pull requests tab → Files changed → Review changes |
| Merge a PR | Approve → Merge pull request → Confirm |
